publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Local generation of multineuronal spike sequences in the hippocampal CA1 region
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the ordered firing of CA1 neurons during ripples is imported from CA3 or assembled locally
span.quote: Although the local origin of the ripple oscillations is well demonstrated ( 25 , 26 ), it has been tacitly assumed that the ripple-associated, sequentially ordered firing of CA1 neurons is synaptically driven by the upstream CA3 cell assemblies ( 12 , 15 ), largely because excitatory recurrent collaterals in the CA1 region are sparse

span.label: whether sequences survive when the usual upstream driver is bypassed and the same neurons are activated directly by light
span.quote: We tested the “local-circuit” hypothesis by comparing the probability of participation and sequential firing of CA1 neurons during theta oscillations, natural spontaneous ripple events, and “synthetic” ripples induced by local optogenetic activation of pyramidal neurons.

span.label: shows that sequence order is partly preserved across theta, spontaneous ripples and optically induced ripples, and that interneuron spiking is what carries the consistency
span.quote: Interneuron spiking was crucial for sequence consistency. These results suggest that participation of single neurons and their sequential order in population events are not strictly determined by extrinsic inputs but also influenced by local-circuit properties, including synapses between local neurons and single-neuron biophysics.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: These results suggest that participation of single neurons and their sequential order in population events are not strictly determined by extrinsic inputs but also influenced by local-circuit properties, including synapses between local neurons and single-neuron biophysics.

span.label: multineuronal spike sequences in hippocampal CA1
span.quote: Sequential activity of multineuronal spiking can be observed during theta and high-frequency ripple oscillations in the hippocampal CA1 region and is linked to experience, but the mechanisms underlying such sequences are unknown.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We recorded a total of 582 well isolated cells from CA1 of four freely moving and six anesthetized mice.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Three sources intersect to produce the sequences: patterned drive from CA3, a wide spread of intrinsic cellular excitability, and heterogeneous local connectivity, the last two making neurons respond unequally to the same extrinsic input
span.quote: We hypothesize that the intersection of three sources of mechanisms explains the observed spike correlations between spontaneous and synthetic ripples as well as their variability: sequential input drive from CA3, wide distribution of intrinsic cellular properties, and differences in local connectivity (the last two leading to unequal responses to extrinsic activation).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Biophysical heterogeneity across pyramidal cells converts even an identical input ramp into diverse spike patterns and hence into a reproducible sequential order
span.quote: Thus, even if every neuron experienced an identical ramp of input current (from the CA3 population during spontaneous ripple events or from the light stimulus during synthetic ripples), diverse spike patterns and sequential activity would still ensue due to intrinsic neuronal/circuit heterogeneity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Each interneuron is driven by a limited set of pyramidal assemblies and silences the competing assemblies, which places it at a fixed point in the sequence and gives pyramidal spiking a temporal scaffold
span.quote: Single interneurons are typically controlled by a limited number of pyramidal cell assemblies ( 35 , 36 ) and suppress the competing assemblies, which can explain their orderly presence in the sequential patterns.

span.label: even if every neuron received an identical ramp of input current, diverse and sequential spiking would still follow from intrinsic neuronal and circuit heterogeneity
span.quote: Thus, even if every neuron experienced an identical ramp of input current (from the CA3 population during spontaneous ripple events or from the light stimulus during synthetic ripples), diverse spike patterns and sequential activity would still ensue due to intrinsic neuronal/circuit heterogeneity.

span.label: interneurons are each controlled by a few pyramidal assemblies and suppress the rest, which is why they appear in orderly positions
span.quote: Single interneurons are typically controlled by a limited number of pyramidal cell assemblies ( 35 , 36 ) and suppress the competing assemblies, which can explain their orderly presence in the sequential patterns. In turn, interneuron spiking may provide a scaffold – a temporal backbone – for pyramidal cell spiking.

span.label: the proposal is a three-way intersection: sequential drive from CA3, spread of intrinsic cellular properties, and differences in local connectivity
span.quote: We hypothesize that the intersection of three sources of mechanisms explains the observed spike correlations between spontaneous and synthetic ripples as well as their variability: sequential input drive from CA3, wide distribution of intrinsic cellular properties, and differences in local connectivity (the last two leading to unequal responses to extrinsic activation).

span.label: the preexisting order may itself be the residue of earlier experience or of development, which the design cannot separate
span.quote: The preexisting sequences may themselves reflect the local circuit configurations shaped by previous experiences, by the developmental genetic program, or any combination thereof.

span.label: Only a limited number of pyramidal cells could be monitored with silicon probes; larger ensemble recordings are needed to test the hypothesis.
span.quote: It may well be that many more pyramidal neurons took part in the sequential patterning of activity than those monitored here by the silicon probes; recordings of larger ensembles of pyramidal cells in future experiments are needed to address this hypothesis.

span.label: The theta/ripple correlation results on their own cannot separate a CA3 from a CA1 origin of the sequences.
span.quote: Sequences may be generated by the upstream CA3 region or locally in CA1 but these results alone cannot disambiguate the contributions of the two regions.

span.label: The measured sequence consistency is loose - rank correlations were widely spread and rarely above 0.5.
span.quote: Thus, although rank correlations were widely distributed and rarely exceeded values of 0.5 (during theta, ripples, and induced ripples) indicating relatively loose self- and cross-class consistency of multineuronal sequences, the observations are robust to the choice of analysis method.

span.label: the theta-ripple correlation alone cannot disambiguate the contributions of CA3 and of CA1
span.quote: Sequences may be generated by the upstream CA3 region or locally in CA1 but these results alone cannot disambiguate the contributions of the two regions.

span.label: far more pyramidal cells probably participate than the probes could record, and larger ensembles are needed
span.quote: It may well be that many more pyramidal neurons took part in the sequential patterning of activity than those monitored here by the silicon probes; recordings of larger ensembles of pyramidal cells in future experiments are needed to address this hypothesis.

span.label: with pyramidal cells alone the cross-class correlation is not significant - though the paper notes the same holds within a single condition
span.quote: When only sequences of pyramidal neurons were considered, the correlation between spontaneous and induced oscillations was not significant. However, this was also the case when sequence patterns were correlated within the same conditions.

span.label: whether the preexisting order reflects experience or development is not addressed
span.quote: The preexisting sequences may themselves reflect the local circuit configurations shaped by previous experiences, by the developmental genetic program, or any combination thereof.

span.label: rank-order templates with permutation-based significance, used so that sequence order can be tested without assuming timing distributions
span.quote: To this end, we rank ordered the spikes of all pyramidal cells and interneurons that occurred in a given event ( Fig. 4 A ), and determined the consistency of multineuronal spiking across events ( Fig. 4 B ); because induced ripples were focal (one site was illuminated at a time; Fig. 2 Ac ), this analysis was done on a site-by-site basis.

span.label: direct local activation used specifically to bypass the upstream input whose contribution is in question
span.quote: We tested the “local-circuit” hypothesis by comparing the probability of participation and sequential firing of CA1 neurons during theta oscillations, natural spontaneous ripple events, and “synthetic” ripples induced by local optogenetic activation of pyramidal neurons.

span.label: synthetic ripple is the same construct Stark2014 named iHFO and Wu2015 reused - an optically induced high-frequency oscillation, kept terminologically apart from the spontaneous ripple throughout
span.quote: We tested the “local-circuit” hypothesis by comparing the probability of participation and sequential firing of CA1 neurons during theta oscillations, natural spontaneous ripple events, and “synthetic” ripples induced by local optogenetic activation of pyramidal neurons.

span.label: sequence consistency here is a RANK correlation between the firing order in one event and a template built from other events, so it measures order and not timing
span.quote: To this end, we rank ordered the spikes of all pyramidal cells and interneurons that occurred in a given event ( Fig. 4 A ), and determined the consistency of multineuronal spiking across events ( Fig. 4 B ); because induced ripples were focal (one site was illuminated at a time; Fig. 2 Ac ), this analysis was done on a site-by-site basis.

span.label: self-consistency (order repeats within a class of events) and cross-class consistency (order carries between classes) are different measures, and the paper's claim rests on the second
span.quote: Sequences during spontaneous and induced ripples were not independent: 13 of 26 induced sequences (50%, P < 0.001) were consistent with their same-site spontaneous counterparts, with a median rank correlation of 0.13

span.label: spike gain is the same within-unit ratio used in Wu2015 - rate during the event over baseline rate - so the two records are comparable on this measure
span.quote: To compare the rate modulation during theta and ripples on a neuron-by-neuron basis, we computed a “gain” measure for each unit, defined as the mean spiking rate during an event (ripple or theta cycle), divided by the baseline spiking rate.

span.label: PYR and INT are assigned by a Gaussian mixture model over waveform features, the same classification route as Wu2015
span.quote: Ten mice were used in this study; nine expressed ChR2 in CA1 pyramidal cells under the CaMKII promoter, and one was opsin-free; all mice were implanted with multisite diode probes ( 48 ). Each probe had four or six shanks (intershank spacing, 200 μm) with 8 or 10 sites per shank (intersite spacing, 20 μm), and each shank was associated with an optical fiber coupled to a miniature LED or laser diode. Light stimulation (50- to 70-ms light pulses) was applied on every shank separately during spontaneous behavior in the home cage ( n = 4 mice) or during urethane anesthesia ( n = 6 mice; ref. 49 ). Offline, spikes were sorted and classified as putatitve PYR or INT using a Gaussian mixture model ( 49 ). Spike sequences were detected and compared using a cross-validated template method or an alternate pair-wise method; statistical significance was verified by resampling (permutation test).

span.label: builds-on → The authors' own earlier demonstration (ref. 26) that local optogenetic stimulation of CA1 pyramidal cells induces fast LFP oscillations resembling spontaneous ripples
span.quote: Recently, we demonstrated that local optogenetic stimulation of CA1 pyramidal neurons is sufficient to induce fast LFP oscillations with many properties similar to spontaneously occurring ripples ( 26 ).

span.label: contradicts → The prevailing assumption (refs 4, 12, 16, 21, 23) that CA1 sequential firing during ripples and theta is generated in CA3 recurrent networks and inherited synaptically by CA1
span.quote: Sequential activity of CA1 pyramidal neurons during ripples and in memory tasks during theta oscillations has been implicitly assumed to be generated in the recurrent excitatory networks of the hippocampal CA3 region and inherited through synaptic activity by the CA1 neuronal population ( 4 , 12 , 16 , 21 , 23 ) although direct evidence has not been shown experimentally.

span.label: replicates → A previous study (ref. 34) of the stability of sequential activation of pyramidal cells and interneurons during neocortical slow oscillations
span.quote: Interneurons were embedded in the assembly sequences, similar to a previous study examining the stability of sequential activation of pyramidal cells and interneurons during slow oscillations in the neocortex ( 34 ).

span.label: contradicts → the tacit assumption that CA1 ripple sequences are synaptically inherited from CA3 assemblies
span.quote: Although the local origin of the ripple oscillations is well demonstrated ( 25 , 26 ), it has been tacitly assumed that the ripple-associated, sequentially ordered firing of CA1 neurons is synaptically driven by the upstream CA3 cell assemblies ( 12 , 15 ), largely because excitatory recurrent collaterals in the CA1 region are sparse

span.label: extends → Stark et al. 2014, which showed local optogenetic activation is sufficient to induce ripple-like oscillations
span.quote: We tested the “local-circuit” hypothesis by comparing the probability of participation and sequential firing of CA1 neurons during theta oscillations, natural spontaneous ripple events, and “synthetic” ripples induced by local optogenetic activation of pyramidal neurons.

span.label: critiques → the inference from waking-sleep correlation to experience-induced synaptic plasticity
span.quote: Correlated sequences and pair-wise correlations between waking exploration and sleep are often taken as evidence for experience-induced synaptic plasticity ( 13 – 15 , 45 ). However, preexisting correlations have also been reported between sleep epochs that precede and follow a novel experience (“preplay;” refs. 43 and 46 ). These observations, combined with the present findings using optical activation of hippocampal circuits, indicate that learning-induced effects should be carefully separated from preexisting conditions biased by the intrinsic properties of neurons and the local interactions between pyramidal cells and interneurons

span.label: supports → preplay reports of correlations present before a novel experience
span.quote: However, preexisting correlations have also been reported between sleep epochs that precede and follow a novel experience (“preplay;”

span.label: confirms → neocortical work finding stable pyramidal-interneuron sequences during slow oscillations
span.quote: Sequentially ordered firing patterns are not unique to the hippocampus but also occur in the neocortex during the UP state of slow oscillations ( 34 , 42 ), suggesting that intrinsic neuronal and local-circuit properties may play a similar role in other systems as well.

span.label: synthetic ripples —contrasted-with→ spontaneous ripples
span.quote: However, under the hypothesis of heterogeneous ChR2 distribution and unequal light distribution, no relationship of firing patterns is expected between spontaneous and synthetic ripples.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED (Q-267)) · INT —causes→ consistency
span.quote: Thus, although interneurons comprised only a small subpopulation of the participating units (12%) and were indirectly activated during optical ripple induction, they made an important contribution to the consistency of multineuronal sequences during both spontaneous and induced ripples.

span.label: PYR —distinct-from→ consistency
span.quote: When limiting the participation to PYR, only 4 of 27 sites exhibited consistent sequences during spontaneous ripples (15%, P = 0.04, exact Binomial test) and the median rank correlation was lower (0.04, P = 0.02, signed-rank test). Similarly, only 7 of 22 (32%, P < 0.001; median rank, 0.13, P = 0.23) sequences were consistent during induced ripples, and cross-class consistency fell to chance level

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · consistency —operationalised-as→ permutation test
span.quote: To this end, we rank ordered the spikes of all pyramidal cells and interneurons that occurred in a given event ( Fig. 4 A ), and determined the consistency of multineuronal spiking across events ( Fig. 4 B ); because induced ripples were focal (one site was illuminated at a time; Fig. 2 Ac ), this analysis was done on a site-by-site basis.

span.label: CA3 —causes→ spike sequences
span.quote: Although the local origin of the ripple oscillations is well demonstrated ( 25 , 26 ), it has been tacitly assumed that the ripple-associated, sequentially ordered firing of CA1 neurons is synaptically driven by the upstream CA3 cell assemblies ( 12 , 15 ), largely because excitatory recurrent collaterals in the CA1 region are sparse

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED FROM AN INFERENCE TO THE INTERVENTION IT RESTS ON) · CA1 —causes→ spike sequences
span.quote: These results indicate that mechanisms confined to the CA1 region contribute to both ripple- and theta-associated neuronal sequences. We suggest that sequential spiking patterns observed in the CA1 region in the intact animal arise from the interplay between extrinsic inputs (from CA3 and the entorhinal cortex), local synaptic interactions, and intrinsic cellular conductances.

span.label: entorhinal —distinct-from→ spike sequences
span.quote: Because layer 3 of the entorhinal input to CA1 is not active during ripples ( 33 ), it is unlikely that the entorhinal input is responsible for generating correlated sequences across different states.

span.label: intrinsic properties —causes→ spike sequences
span.quote: Thus, even if every neuron experienced an identical ramp of input current (from the CA3 population during spontaneous ripple events or from the light stimulus during synthetic ripples), diverse spike patterns and sequential activity would still ensue due to intrinsic neuronal/circuit heterogeneity.

span.label: replay —contrasted-with→ preplay
span.quote: Correlated sequences and pair-wise correlations between waking exploration and sleep are often taken as evidence for experience-induced synaptic plasticity ( 13 – 15 , 45 ). However, preexisting correlations have also been reported between sleep epochs that precede and follow a novel experience (“preplay;” refs. 43 and 46 ). These observations, combined with the present findings using optical activation of hippocampal circuits, indicate that learning-induced effects should be carefully separated from preexisting conditions biased by the intrinsic properties of neurons and the local interactions between pyramidal cells and interneurons

span.label: PYR —contrasted-with→ INT
span.quote: The marked increase of PYR relative to INT spiking ( P = 0.01, Mann–Whitney U test) is consistent with direct activation of PYR (and indirect activation of INT) in these animals during induced ripples.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · theta —contrasted-with→ spontaneous ripples
span.quote: To compare the relationship between sequential ordering of neurons during individual ripple events and theta cycles (“cross-class consistency”), we used the spike sequences during ripple events as a template against which spiking during each theta cycle was compared. In 10 of 11 cases (91%, chance level, 5%, P < 0.001, exact Binomial test), the sequences during ripples and theta were similar

span.label: INT —causes→ consistency
span.quote: Including both PYR and INT almost doubles the cross-class sequence consistency.

span.label: consistency —operationalised-as→ permutation test
span.quote: Statistical significance of sequence consistency was determined by a permutation test, randomly shuffling the ranks of the units that participated in each event and carrying out the entire procedure, culminating in the computation of the mean rank correlation.

span.label: theta —contrasted-with→ spontaneous ripples
span.quote: We compared multineuronal spiking during theta oscillations, spontaneous ripples, and focal optically induced high-frequency oscillations (“synthetic” ripples) in freely moving mice.

span.label: CA1 —causes→ spike sequences
span.quote: We show that optogenetic activation of a small group of CA1 pyramidal cells in mouse hippocampus yields consistent multineuronal spike sequences, and that their sequential firing order is similar to that observed during spontaneous “ripple” and theta oscillations.

span.label: rank correlation
span.quote: The firing rates of CA1 pyramidal cells (PYR) and putative interneurons (INT) during theta oscillations and ripple events were correlated (rank correlations: PYR: 0.59, P < 0.001, permutation test; INT: 0.89, P < 0.001; n = 268 PYR and 37 INT recorded from four freely moving mice; Fig. 1 A ).

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: Statistical significance of sequence consistency was determined by a permutation test, randomly shuffling the ranks of the units that participated in each event and carrying out the entire procedure, culminating in the computation of the mean rank correlation.

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Although spike gain was higher during ripples than during theta (median ratio: PYR: 2.8, P < 0.001, Wilcoxon’s signed-rank paired test; INT: 2.2, P < 0.001), the spike gain of PYR during theta and ripples was correlated (rank correlations: PYR: 0.21, P < 0.001; INT: 0.27, P = 0.06; Fig. 1 B ).

span.label: binomial test
span.quote: In 10 of 11 cases (91%, chance level, 5%, P < 0.001, exact Binomial test), the sequences during ripples and theta were similar (median cross-class consistency: 0.21, P < 0.001; Fig. 1 C – E ).

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: The marked increase of PYR relative to INT spiking ( P = 0.01, Mann–Whitney U test) is consistent with direct activation of PYR (and indirect activation of INT) in these animals during induced ripples.

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
span.quote: The median rank correlation was not different for the three datasets (spontaneous-ripple self-consistency; induced-ripple self-consistency; and cross-class consistency of induced-ripple, relative to spontaneous ripple sequences; P = 0.35, Kruskal–Wallis test).

span.label: circular correlation
span.quote: On a neuron-by-neuron basis, the spike phases during spontaneous and induced ripples were correlated (circular–circular correlation coefficient: PYR: 0.7, P < 0.001, χ 2 test; INT: 0.42, P = 0.04; n = 97 PYR and 26 INT phase-locked during both spontaneous and induced ripples; Fig. 3 ).

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: For proportions, the exact Binomial test (single comparisons) and the χ 2 test (pairwise or multiple groups) were used.

span.label: cross-validation
span.quote: In the cross-validated template method, a template for each specific ripple or theta event was constructed based on the averaged rank of all units over all other events (i.e., excluding that specific event).

span.label: Gaussian mixture model
span.quote: Offline, spikes were sorted and classified as putatitve PYR or INT using a Gaussian mixture model ( 49 ).

span.label: principal component analysis
span.quote: Briefly, waveforms were linearly detrended, projected onto a common basis obtained by principal component analysis of the data, and sorted automatically followed by manual adjustment.

span.label: significance level
span.quote: An α level of 0.05 was used throughout.

span.label: permutation test
span.quote: To this end, we rank ordered the spikes of all pyramidal cells and interneurons that occurred in a given event ( Fig. 4 A ), and determined the consistency of multineuronal spiking across events ( Fig. 4 B ); because induced ripples were focal (one site was illuminated at a time; Fig. 2 Ac ), this analysis was done on a site-by-site basis.

span.label: rank correlation
span.quote: The firing rates of CA1 pyramidal cells (PYR) and putative interneurons (INT) during theta oscillations and ripple events were correlated (rank correlations: PYR: 0.59, P < 0.001, permutation test; INT: 0.89, P < 0.001; n = 268 PYR and 37 INT recorded from four freely moving mice

span.label: Wilcoxon
span.quote: During spontaneous ripples, most multineuronal sequences were self-consistent (23 of 27 recording sites, 85%; P < 0.001, exact Binomial test), with a median rank correlation of 0.28

span.label: exact Binomial test
span.quote: When limiting the participation to PYR, only 4 of 27 sites exhibited consistent sequences during spontaneous ripples (15%, P = 0.04, exact Binomial test) and the median rank correlation was lower (0.04, P = 0.02, signed-rank test). Similarly, only 7 of 22 (32%, P < 0.001; median rank, 0.13, P = 0.23) sequences were consistent during induced ripples, and cross-class consistency fell to chance level

span.label: Rayleigh test
span.quote: Most units (224 of 268 PYR, 84%; 34 of 37 INT, 95%) exhibited consistent locking to ripple phase ( P < 0.05, Rayleigh test), and phase-locked PYR spiked consistently earlier than phase-locked INT (mean± SEM phases: PYR: 156 ± 1.7°, INT: 254 ± 6.7°; corresponding to time lag of 1.8 ± 0.2 ms

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: The marked increase of PYR relative to INT spiking ( P = 0.01, Mann–Whitney U test) is consistent with direct activation of PYR (and indirect activation of INT) in these animals during induced ripples.

span.label: Individual neurons' firing rates, their rate modulation, and the order in which pyramidal cells and interneurons fired were all correlated across three different network states: theta oscillations, spontaneous ripples, and optogenetically induced ripples.
span.quote: Firing rates and rate modulations of individual neurons, and multineuronal sequences of pyramidal cell and interneuron spiking, were correlated during theta oscillations, spontaneous ripples, and synthetic ripples.

span.label: Because sequences recur during locally induced ripples that receive no CA3 or entorhinal patterning, the sequential order of CA1 spiking cannot be purely inherited from upstream regions and must partly arise from CA1's own circuitry and single-cell biophysics.
span.quote: Thus, multineuronal spike sequences are not exclusively inherited from upstream sources but result from local-circuit dynamics and biophysical properties of the individual neurons.

span.label: Half of the optogenetically induced spike sequences matched the spontaneous ripple sequence recorded at the same site, with a median rank correlation of 0.13.
span.quote: Sequences during spontaneous and induced ripples were not independent: 13 of 26 induced sequences (50%, P < 0.001) were consistent with their same-site spontaneous counterparts, with a median rank correlation of 0.13 ( P < 0.001; 0.21 for the consistent sequences; Fig. 4 D ).

span.label: Interneurons made up only 12% of the participating units and were only indirectly driven by the light, yet dropping them from the analysis destroyed the cross-state consistency of the sequences, so they are essential to sequence structure.
span.quote: Thus, although interneurons comprised only a small subpopulation of the participating units (12%) and were indirectly activated during optical ripple induction, they made an important contribution to the consistency of multineuronal sequences during both spontaneous and induced ripples.

span.label: With pyramidal cells alone the correlation between theta-cycle and ripple sequence order dropped to chance, so the shared ordering across states depends on including interneurons.
span.quote: However, when only PYR (median, 22; range, 6–51) were considered, the median cross-class consistency fell to chance level ( P = 0.83; Fig. 1 G ).

span.label: The preferred firing phase of each unit within the ripple cycle was the same for spontaneous and light-induced ripples, so cycle-level spike timing is conserved between the two.
span.quote: Therefore, the precise temporal relations between single unit spiking and ripple cycles are preserved during spontaneous and induced ripples.

span.label: Sequence consistency was real but weak: rank correlations were broadly spread and seldom above 0.5, and the same conclusions followed whether a template or a pairwise comparison method was used.
span.quote: Thus, although rank correlations were widely distributed and rarely exceeded values of 0.5 (during theta, ripples, and induced ripples) indicating relatively loose self- and cross-class consistency of multineuronal sequences, the observations are robust to the choice of analysis method.

span.label: Under urethane anaesthesia, sequences were self-consistent within each event class but spontaneous and induced sequences did not match each other, unlike in freely moving mice.
span.quote: Spontaneous and induced (cross-class) sequences are not consistent.

span.label: firing rates during theta and during ripples were correlated neuron by neuron
span.quote: The firing rates of CA1 pyramidal cells (PYR) and putative interneurons (INT) during theta oscillations and ripple events were correlated (rank correlations: PYR: 0.59, P < 0.001, permutation test; INT: 0.89, P < 0.001; n = 268 PYR and 37 INT recorded from four freely moving mice

span.label: sequences recorded during ripples matched those during theta cycles in 10 of 11 sessions
span.quote: To compare the relationship between sequential ordering of neurons during individual ripple events and theta cycles (“cross-class consistency”), we used the spike sequences during ripple events as a template against which spiking during each theta cycle was compared. In 10 of 11 cases (91%, chance level, 5%, P < 0.001, exact Binomial test), the sequences during ripples and theta were similar

span.label: spike phase within the cycle was preserved between spontaneous and induced ripples
span.quote: On a neuron-by-neuron basis, the spike phases during spontaneous and induced ripples were correlated (circular–circular correlation coefficient: PYR: 0.7, P < 0.001, χ 2 test; INT: 0.42, P = 0.04; n = 97 PYR and 26 INT phase-locked during both spontaneous and induced ripples; Fig. 3 ). Therefore, the precise temporal relations between single unit spiking and ripple cycles are preserved during spontaneous and induced ripples.

span.label: pyramidal cells fired about 1.8 ms before interneurons on each ripple cycle
span.quote: Most units (224 of 268 PYR, 84%; 34 of 37 INT, 95%) exhibited consistent locking to ripple phase ( P < 0.05, Rayleigh test), and phase-locked PYR spiked consistently earlier than phase-locked INT (mean± SEM phases: PYR: 156 ± 1.7°, INT: 254 ± 6.7°; corresponding to time lag of 1.8 ± 0.2 ms

span.label: sequences repeated across spontaneous ripple events at 23 of 27 recording sites
span.quote: During spontaneous ripples, most multineuronal sequences were self-consistent (23 of 27 recording sites, 85%; P < 0.001, exact Binomial test), with a median rank correlation of 0.28

span.label: half the induced sequences matched their own site's spontaneous sequences
span.quote: Sequences during spontaneous and induced ripples were not independent: 13 of 26 induced sequences (50%, P < 0.001) were consistent with their same-site spontaneous counterparts, with a median rank correlation of 0.13

span.label: theta sequences and induced-ripple sequences also matched, at 10 of 25 sites
span.quote: Sequences during individual theta cycles and induced ripples were also interdependent: 10 of 25 (40%, P < 0.001) sites exhibited theta vs. induced ripples cross-class consistency, with a median rank correlation of 0.17 ( P < 0.001; 0.32 for the consistent sequences; Fig. S4 ). Thus, sequences observed during spontaneous theta or ripple oscillations and induced ripples are similar, indicating that despite being driven by very different inputs (medial septum-associated theta, CA3-associated SPW, and local optically induced ChR2 activation), spiking during these three constellations share some common generative mechanisms.

span.label: with pyramidal cells alone, cross-class consistency fell to chance; with interneurons alone it survived
span.quote: When limiting participation to INT, sequences were still consistent ( Fig. 5 B ), and cross-class consistency was 1.75 times lower than when all neurons were considered ( P = 0.55, paired signed-rank test; rank correlation: 0.54, P < 0.001), suggesting that rate difference between PYR and INT and/or intrinsic PYR-INT correlations are not accountable for the observed consistency.

span.label: interneurons are 12% of the units and carry the consistency
span.quote: Thus, although interneurons comprised only a small subpopulation of the participating units (12%) and were indirectly activated during optical ripple induction, they made an important contribution to the consistency of multineuronal sequences during both spontaneous and induced ripples.

span.label: in the pyramidal-only session analysis three sessions were consistent and three were REVERSED, so the group mean describes neither
span.quote: On a session-by-session basis, 6 of 11 (55%; P < 0.001) sessions exhibited significant rank correlations, although half were consistent (3 of 11, 27%, P = 0.02; median cross-class consistency: 0.05) and half were reversed (3 of 11, 27%, P = 0.02; median, -0.04;

span.label: CONTROL NULL: illumination of an opsin-free mouse produced no spikes, no oscillations and no artefact
span.quote: In contrast to the effect in opsin-expressing mice (compare to Fig. 2 in the main text; also see refs. 26 , 48 , and 49 ), note lack of consistent modulation (activation or suppression) during focal illumination, indicating that diode-probe illumination by itself does not induce thermal, optical, or electromagnetic modulation of neural activity.

span.label: CONTROL: induced-ripple rates track spontaneous rates, so the induced pattern is not set by opsin level or distance from the light
span.quote: Thus, firing rates and their modulations during induced ripples are not an arbitrary outcome of opsin- or optics-dependent parameters (expression level, distance from light source).

span.label: spontaneous and induced ripples occurred in the same brain state at the same rate
span.quote: Although only about half of the time was spent in NTI (55% ± 4%), both spontaneous and induced ripples occurred predominantly during that state (83% ± 4% and 75% ± 7%, respectively; P = 0.33, t test).

span.label: SCOPE TO CHECK: the main text reports similar results under anaesthesia, and the supplementary caption it cites states cross-class sequences are NOT consistent there
span.quote: Similar results were observed under anesthesia (separate cohort of n = 5 urethane-anesthetized mice; Fig. S3 ). Thus, multineuronal spike sequences during induced ripples are not random.
